doc.title: John Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001

title: Moving to St. Petersburg and teaching career
summary: He chooses St. Petersburg, tries insurance and the Tampa orchestra, plays hotels and teaches school for 27 years.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well, since those years you’ve remained, made your living as a musician and how did you end up back in Florida?

Well we were reading a series of articles about life in Sarasota. And I had attended the college and I had been there five years and I had gotten my double degree and I taught in Philly for a couple of years in the prep department at the school as well as Ripple School. So we hopped in the car and we drove down to Sarasota and Miami and all those places. And we checked the places out. We decided that Sarasota was not it for us, so we came back up to St. Petersburg and discovered that that’s where Buster Cooper lived, my old road buddy. And we says well Buster lives here, and this is centrally located, Tampa is here, Clearwater is here, Sarasota is here, this is the place to be. So we decided on St. Petersburg. And on top of that I wanted my kids to grow up with the proper attitude. I didn’t want them to have to fight their way to school and back, you know, in the inner city, like a lot a problems can happen like that with other kids and groups and that type of thing.
How many kids did you have?

Two. And so that’s how we ended up down here. The kids, plus I had the ability to teach now, I’ve had the license to teach, so I came down and went into the insurance business for a year, and they says, “are you crazy?” Well I could still play a little bit, and then I decided after a year that that wasn’t for me, and decided that I would get into the orchestra. So I played with the orchestra, the Tampa Bay Orchestra. And my wife and kids were there the first night, opening night. But I soon discovered that wasn’t for me because we’d rehearse and rehearse and rehearse the same thing over and over again, and then the conductor would go crazy sometimes, and all for $25, you know what I mean, for a rehearsal. And I discovered I could come back over to the hotel and make maybe $250 a week or so and just have a great time. So I did that. And also during that time I played with the Opera House here for about two or three years, got that little experience under my belt. And in the meantime I got this gig teaching high school. I taught high school, and when that came along I got a job teaching at the junior college. The word began to get around. And I began to teach the different schools, and then I went to middle school and stayed there over 20 years, and I retired after 25 years in a middle school, 27 years all total teaching. © Fillius Jazz Archive -27-
